summary: Source-anchored research for WiredTiger Compaction Algorithm. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: The available-extent structure has indexes by address and size; compaction selects first-fit allocation to favor earlier file offsets. (high confidence)

The B-tree walk can relocate an uncached leaf directly at the block-manager layer, avoiding loading and reconciling it through cache; its parent receives the new address and becomes dirty. (high confidence)

A December 2024 operator report on MongoDB 6.0.19 recorded repeated EBUSY retries and zero-rewrite messages over a long compaction run; the thread does not establish a verified root cause. (low confidence)

In the inspected develop code, files at most 1 MiB are skipped; the first iteration also skips when live available bytes are below free_space_target. Passing the configured threshold does not bypass the spatial eligibility test. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
Tail-focused passes matter because the Btree walk follows logical order: moving earlier live blocks first could consume destinations needed to evacuate the file tail. (medium confidence)

In the inspected develop code, compaction stops if the file grows between passes; once estimation is active, unchanged rewritten-page counts also cause a no-progress skip. Therefore repeated attempts have no unconditional reclamation guarantee. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Percona's July 17, 2024 article reports that a compact command can return OK while physical size stays unchanged because WiredTiger decides there is no useful compaction work. This is an operational observation, not proof that another invocation must reclaim space. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-07-17)

The inspected develop eligibility test requires available bytes exceeding 1 MiB and reaching 20% of total file size in the initial 80%, otherwise exceeding 1 MiB and reaching 10% of total size in the initial 90%; it selects the corresponding tail region. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
WT-9629 documents missing progress-statistic updates in direct block relocation; zero reported rewrites on affected builds therefore cannot establish that no blocks moved. (low confidence)

Compaction moves selected blocks from the file tail into earlier reusable space; filesystem reclamation requires a free tail that can be truncated. It is best effort and can succeed without reducing file size. (medium confidence)

In the inspected develop code, a candidate block must lie beyond the selected tail boundary and have an earlier available extent large enough to hold it. The existence check uses by-size buckets; this is distinct from first-fit allocation. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
Cached leaves selected for relocation are marked dirty; checkpoint or eviction rewrites them and their dirty ancestor pages. (low confidence)

After a compaction pass, two further checkpoints allow newly freed blocks to pass through checkpoint-available bookkeeping and become usable for subsequent checkpoint writes near the file front. Immediate reuse before the metadata update would compromise crash safety. (medium confidence)

A named checkpoint that still references a tail block can prevent truncation even after that block is rewritten; the checkpoint must be explicitly removed or replaced before its references disappear. (medium confidence)
The inspected develop implementation skips further work after estimation if the rewritten-page count has not increased since the preceding iteration. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
Percona's PSMDB 6.0.14 experiment reported 507662336 bytes freed while retaining 34000896 bytes available for reuse, illustrating that compaction can leave reusable space behind. (low confidence)

A 2018 UBC study's compaction example attributed a performance drop to asynchronous worker threads spinning for work; that historical test observation does not establish the behavior of current background compaction. (low confidence)
In the inspected develop code, compaction switches allocation to first-fit at start and restores the prior allocation plan at end. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Compaction walks internal pages and evaluates referenced leaves. On-disk leaves can move through block-manager I/O without entering the WiredTiger page cache; cached eligible pages are marked for rewriting, and changed child addresses require parent updates. (medium confidence)

The inspected block rewrite path reads the original block into a scratch buffer, allocates and writes a replacement, frees the original block, and returns an address cookie containing the new offset and original checksum. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

Compaction normally starts with a database-wide checkpoint to expose reusable blocks; background compaction skips this initial checkpoint to reduce checkpoint work. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)

The inspected Btree compaction walk checks for interruption and stuck eviction, can return EBUSY, and assists eviction to throttle its cache intake; a checkpoint flush-lock conflict is retried while checking those exit conditions. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-30)
